title: Your data is yours
lead: Impact log runs on your device and encrypts entries before they go anywhere. An account is only needed for sync — and even then the server sees nothing but ciphertext. Here’s an honest, detailed account of what is stored where, and how.

localFirst.title: Your device first
localFirst.text: The app works without signing up: entries live in an encrypted vault in your browser. An account is only needed to sync devices.

e2ee.title: End-to-end encryption
e2ee.text: Entries are encrypted on your device with a key we don’t have. Your password, Master Key and Recovery Key never reach the server in the clear — even the server admin can’t read your entries.

minimal.title: Minimal data
minimal.text: Sync needs only a username and password. We don’t ask for email, phone or name, and we don’t try to find out who you are.

noTracking.title: No tracking
noTracking.text: No analytics, telemetry, trackers, ads or emails. We don’t know what you click, and we don’t want to.

yours.title: Your data belongs to you
yours.text: Full export at any time, on any plan. Account deletion is immediate and complete — no trash bins.

honest.title: No fine print
honest.text: If something isn’t there yet, we say so. Any change in how we handle data shows up on this page right away.

device.title: On your device
device.lead: All of this is stored in your browser. Without sync, nothing goes to the server and it knows nothing about you. With sync, the server gets only encrypted copies of entries and what’s listed under “What the server sees”.

records.how: Text, date, categories, labels, metrics, artifact links — in the browser’s IndexedDB, encrypted only (in the same format that goes to the server when you sync).

masterKey.how: Stored on disk only wrapped by the device key. Open in the tab’s memory while you work.

deviceKey.how: A non-extractable AES-256-GCM key (WebCrypto): the browser lets the app use it but never hands its bytes to any JavaScript — not even impact log’s own code.

account.how: If sync is on: your username, Account ID, this device’s id and secret, the key epoch (the number of your account’s current Master Key), plus the password salt and protection settings from your last sign-in. The browser presents the device id and secret only when signing in (the server keeps just a hash of the secret), and the salt and settings help notice if they suddenly get weaker on the server.

conflicts.how: If an entry was changed on two devices at once, a copy of the server version is kept here next to yours (encrypted) until you choose which one to keep. Such entries are marked “Version conflict” in the journal and on the entry screen.

quarantine.how: If an entry can’t be decrypted when you sign in to an account (corruption, a foreign key), it isn’t lost and doesn’t block sign-in: its ciphertext is set aside on this device and never sent anywhere. In Settings → Data you can download it as is or delete it.

pendingRotation.how: Only while an encryption key change started on this device is in progress: the new Master Key is kept here wrapped by the device key — just like the current one — so the change can be resumed after a reload without your password. It’s removed as soon as the change completes or is cancelled.

prefs.how: The browser’s localStorage holds settings only: theme, language and review report layout. No entries or keys.

draft.how: It arrives in the page address (/capture#draft=…), so the link may stay in your browser history. Until you save the entry (including while you sign in), the draft sits in this tab’s sessionStorage; it is removed once saved. Of a saved draft, only its id and a pointer to the entry stay on the device — so reopening the same link does not create a duplicate.

swCache.how: The browser keeps impact log’s code and design (scripts, styles, fonts, icons) in the service worker cache, so the app opens and works offline. Your entries and keys are not in this cache: requests to the server don’t go through it and aren’t stored. Each new version replaces the cache entirely.

masterKey.title: Master Key
masterKey.text: 256 random bits, created on your device and not derived from your password. You can change your password without re-encrypting entries. And the Master Key itself can be changed in Settings → Security: every entry is re-encrypted with the new key, each with a new key of its own.

objects.title: AES-256-GCM for every entry
objects.text: Each entry has its own random key, wrapped by the Master Key. The ciphertext is bound to the entry id — the server can’t silently swap one entry for another.

password.title: Argon2id, 64 MiB
password.text: Your browser derives two independent keys from your password (Argon2id: 64 MiB of memory, 3 passes, a unique salt): the KEK opens the Master Key envelope, the authKey proves sign-in. Only the authKey goes to the server — the KEK can’t be derived from it.

device.title: Device key
device.text: On every device the Master Key is wrapped by a non-extractable browser key: it exists in the clear only in the memory of an open tab. This doesn’t protect against someone with full access to your computer — use disk encryption and a screen lock.

server.title: What the server sees
server.lead: Only if you turned on sync. This is the complete list — if something isn’t here, we don’t store it.

account.how: Username, Account ID (random, says nothing about you), plan, creation date.

password.how: We don’t have your password. We store an Argon2id hash of authKey, plus the salt and KDF settings so your browser can repeat the key derivation. The browser remembers them and warns you if at the next sign-in they turn out weaker or change without you.

keys.how: The Master Key encrypted with your password, and the Master Key encrypted with your Recovery Key — for the current key epoch (the Master Key’s number, which grows with each encryption key change). Without the password or key nobody can open them — neither we nor anyone else.

rotation.how: Only while an encryption key change is in progress — a temporary draft: copies of entries re-encrypted with the new key (also ciphertext, with the entry id and version), envelopes of the new Master Key and a hash of the new Recovery Key, when it started and which device started it. Once confirmed, the draft replaces the old ciphertexts and envelopes; if cancelled, it’s deleted.

recovery.how: Only a SHA-256 of the derived recoveryAuthKey — to check the key during recovery. If a recovery without password and 2FA has been started, also when it started: to hold the 48 hours and warn your signed-in devices. We never see the key itself.

totp.how: The secret for app codes, encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a key stored separately from the database.

records.how: Opaque ciphertext (up to 256 KiB) with the entry id, version number, key epoch, change time and a deletion flag. They reveal the size and timing of changes, not the content.

devices.how: A name encrypted with your key, when it was added and last active, a hash of the device secret (so no other session can pose as your device), the “remembered” mark (token hash and expiry), revocation.

sessions.how: Session token hash, its kind and expiry, the count of wrong 2FA codes.

recovery.title: Recovery Key: without it, data can’t be recovered
recovery.text: When you turn on sync, your browser creates a Recovery Key (ILRK1-…, 160 random bits). It opens a second Master Key envelope, but the key alone isn’t enough to get into the account — you need one more factor: forgot your password — the key and a 2FA code; lost your phone — your password and the key. Without a second factor, recovery is only possible after 48 hours: all that time your signed-in devices show a warning and can cancel it. We have no email, so the warning is shown only in the app. We can’t reset your password: we have neither your password nor the key to your data.
recovery.warning: If you lose both your password and your Recovery Key, nobody can recover the data on the server — not even us. Entries already open on your devices stay available: export them and start over.

capture.title: Quick capture from the extension, CLI and VS Code
capture.text: The draft reaches the app in the page address, in the link fragment (/capture#draft=…). Browsers never send the fragment to the server, and the app removes it from the address bar right away. Still, the link with the draft may stay in your browser history, like any address you open. The entry is encrypted only when you save it.

items.webCode: The web app is loaded from the server, so you trust the code it serves: a server serving malicious code could read entries in an open tab. This is a general limit of encryption in web apps. We reduce the risk with a strict CSP and no third-party scripts, but there are no signed builds yet.
items.rotation: Changing the encryption key protects the future, not the past. A revoked or compromised device can’t read entries created or changed afterwards, and the old password envelope and old Recovery Key, together with old copies of the data, won’t open the new ones. But entries already downloaded to another device or copied stay there: what was read can’t be un-read. Changing your password doesn’t change the encryption key.
items.recoveryKey: The Recovery Key is a decryption key. The 48-hour delay protects access to the account, not the data: whoever has both the key and the ciphertext (for example, from a database leak) can read your entries right away. And if nobody opens the app on a signed-in device during those 48 hours, nobody sees the warning. Keep the key offline, separate from your password; if it may have fallen into the wrong hands, change the encryption key — the old Recovery Key won’t open the new data.
items.knownDevice: On a known device the vault opens without a password: your entries are protected by the browser profile and your OS account. Use a screen lock and disk encryption.
items.revoke: Revoking a device stops its sync but doesn’t erase data already downloaded to it. To make sure it can’t read new or changed entries, change the encryption key after revoking it.

cookies.title: Cookies
cookies.lead: Without sync — none at all. With sync — only technical ones, no ads or tracking:

session.how: Session. HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict, sent only to /api. Lasts until the browser closes (one day, extended while in use) or 30 days if you checked “Remember this computer”. The database keeps only a hash.

device.how: Only with “Remember this computer”: for 30 days, sign-in on this device without a 2FA code (the password is always required). Sent only to /api/auth, the database keeps a hash. Reset by “sign out everywhere”, account recovery (including signing in with the Recovery Key instead of a 2FA code) and device revocation.

items.name: Name or other personal data
items.sale: Anything to sell or share with third parties

location.title: Server in Russia
location.text: Encrypted sync data is stored on a single server in a Moscow data center. No cloud data processing services.

transport.title: Secure connection
transport.text: HTTPS only with HSTS, a strict Content Security Policy, and rate limits on sign-in and code attempts.

logs.title: Technical logs
logs.text: Time, method and path of a request, response code and a truncated IP (IPv4 to /24, IPv6 to /48). No headers, cookies or request bodies. Size-based rotation: only the latest records are kept (up to 5 files of 10 MB).

alpha.title: Alpha stage
alpha.text: The service is in active development. Regular server backups are still being set up — keep an export of your entries at hand.

items.export: Full export of entries to JSON, CSV and Markdown — always, on any plan (Settings → Data). Export files are not encrypted: keep them as carefully as the entries themselves.
items.wipe: Wipe data from a device: entries are removed from this browser but stay on the server and your other devices.
items.delete: Account deletion: the server immediately deletes the account, key envelopes, devices, sessions and all encrypted entries — no trash bins or delayed retention.
items.devices: A list of devices, revoking any of them, and signing out everywhere.
items.rotation: Changing the encryption key: a new Master Key, every entry re-encrypted, a new Recovery Key issued, and your other devices ask you to sign in again.
items.aiPrompt: “Prompt for your own AI” on the review screen is only copied to the clipboard: you decide where to paste it, the app sends nothing anywhere.
items.ai: AI features, if they appear, only with explicit consent and a warning that entry text will be sent to an external provider.

source.title: The source code is public — check for yourself
source.text: Everything on this page can be verified in the code: what the server stores, how entries are encrypted, what the browser sends over the network and how the code gets to impact-log.com. You don’t have to take our word for it. The code is licensed under GNU AGPL-3.0: anyone running a modified version as a service must offer its source code to its users.
